details:
**Gambling with Khonsu for five extra days**
Ra had forbidden the sky goddess Nut from giving birth on any day of the year. Thoth played a game (often said to be senet) against the moon god Khonsu and won a portion (one seventy-second) of the moon's light, which he used to create five extra days outside the 360-day year. On these epagomenal days Nut gave birth to Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis, and Nephthys, completing the 365-day calendar.

**Ibis head and baboon form (A'an)**
Thoth is usually shown as a man with the head of an ibis, a long-beaked wading bird, whose curved beak was linked to the crescent moon. He was also depicted as a dog-faced baboon, notably in his form A'an, the god of equilibrium; both animals were sacred to him.

**Scribe at the weighing of the heart**
In the judgment of the dead in the Hall of Ma'at (Hall of Two Truths), Thoth stands beside the scales on which Anubis weighs the dead person's heart against the feather of Ma'at. He records the result on his scribe's palette and announces the verdict.

**Hermes Trismegistus and Hermopolis**
The Greeks identified Thoth with Hermes, and the fusion produced Hermes Trismegistus ("thrice-great Hermes"), the legendary author of the Hermetic writings. Thoth's cult center was Khmun in Middle Egypt, which the Greeks called Hermopolis ("city of Hermes").

**Ma'at and Seshat**
Ma'at, goddess of truth, justice, and cosmic order, is often called Thoth's consort or feminine counterpart, and the two stand together on the sun god's boat. Seshat, the goddess of writing and measurement who wears a leopard skin, is described as either his wife or his daughter and helped him create writing.

**Book of Thoth**
A legendary book of magic written by Thoth containing two powerful spells, one granting understanding of the speech of animals and power over heaven and earth, the other allowing one to see the gods. In the Egyptian tale of Setne Khamwas, Prince Neferkaptah retrieved it from the Nile near Coptos, where it lay in a gold box nested inside other boxes and guarded by serpents; it was later buried with him in his tomb.

**Helping Isis resurrect Osiris**
After Set murdered and dismembered Osiris, Thoth, as the master of magic, gave Isis the magic words needed to reassemble and revive her husband. He also gave her incantations to heal the infant Horus.

**Restoring the Eye of Horus**
During the struggle between Horus and Set, Set tore out or injured Horus's (left) eye. Thoth healed and restored it; the restored eye, the wedjat, became a symbol of protection and wholeness and was linked to the waxing and waning moon.

**Arbiter between Horus and Set**
As a god of mediation and law, Thoth judged disputes between gods, especially the contest between Horus and Set for Osiris's throne. When Set ate lettuce covered in Horus's semen, Thoth summoned the semen, which emerged from Set's head as a golden sun disk that Thoth took and wore on his own head.

**Seven scorpions and the healing of Horus**
In one myth, Thoth sent seven scorpions to protect Isis while she hid from Set in the marshes. In another, he helped heal the infant Horus after he was stung by a scorpion.

**Ra's solar barque and Apep**
Thoth stood with Ma'at on either side of Ra's solar boat as it traveled across the sky and through the underworld each night. He helped defend Ra against the chaos serpent Apep (Apophis).

**Bringing Tefnut back from Nubia**
In the myth of the "Distant Goddess," Tefnut (or the Eye of Ra) fled angrily to Nubia in the form of a lioness, leaving Egypt dry. Thoth, sometimes with Shu, was sent to calm her and persuade her to return.

**Inventor of writing and "Tongue of Ra"**
Thoth was credited with inventing hieroglyphic writing and was the patron of scribes, as well as a god of magic, mathematics, astronomy, and knowledge; he was also called the "Tongue of Ra." He was considered the author of spells in the Book of the Dead.

**Creator god of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad**
In the cosmology of Hermopolis, centered on the Ogdoad, a group of eight primordial deities, Thoth was sometimes regarded as a creator god. Originally a lunar deity, he was sometimes identified or conflated with the moon god Khonsu.

**Identification with Moses (Artapanus)**
The Hellenistic Jewish writer Artapanus of Alexandria claimed that Moses was the one the Egyptians honored as Thoth (Hermes), presenting Moses as the source of Egyptian learning and culture.
